newsitem.title: GERMANY: Car, bank shares buoy German DAX at opening.
newsitem.headline: Car, bank shares buoy German DAX at opening.

text.p: Ongoing interest in car and bank stocks supported the German share market in early dealings on Thursday, but caution ahead of the Easter holiday was seen capping gains.

"People shouldn't really be making any major bets right now, especially since Wall Street will be open while we are closed," said a Munich dealer. German markets are closed for Easter from Friday through Monday.

The 30-share DAX started the day up 16.06 points at 3,434.18 points, partly playing catch-up with strong gains in post-bourse electronic dealings Wednesday afternoon, when Daimler-Benz unexpectedly issued results for 1996 showing a strong recovery from 1995's unprecedented losses.
"Those numbers were really well above what people expected. They had an even bigger impact because they weren't expected at all until next month," said a Frankfurt dealer.

Daimler reported net profit of 2.9 billion marks and pledged to resume a dividend payout, which it dropped the previous year. Its shares surged and were up 3.5 percent and 136.30 points on Thursday morning.
Rival BMW, also benefiting from strong earnings data issued earlier this week, was up 4.2 percent at 360 marks.

Bank stocks also remained in the limelight, amid a fresh rush of merger speculation and after a positive earnings outlook from market leader Deutsche Bank, which said its business in early 1997 had gone very well.
The DAX-100 bank index, which measures banking stocks among the top 100 German shares, was up nearly three percent. Deutsche was up 73 pfennigs at 94.40 marks.

"Everyone wants into banks again all at once," commented one trader. "Although we've seen this week what we can expect from hostile takeover attempts in Germany," he added, referring to the aborted steel industry takeover bid by Krupp for Thyssen.
Thyssen shares were slightly lower, down two marks at 373 marks, after it and Krupp finalised their co-operation, with a steel venture to be 60 percent controlled by Thyssen.

The news has generally been viewed as a negative for the German market, which had perked up at the chance of an Anglo-Saxon style takeover, but also revived talk of consolidation in the overcrowded banking industry.
